s.d: examination or observation of what is outside oneself, as opposed to introspection.
x: The botanist is a ceremonial sort, his extrospection the work of a husbandman of the mind.

s.d: (uncountable) The observation of things external to one's own mind, as opposed to introspection. Ordinary sense perception or reasoning concerning the things perceived.
not introspective; examining what is outside yourself
Involving extrospection.
x: When it comes to understanding the subjective self, Kohut (1959) sees the introspective and extrospective methods as unequal in value.

extroversion.e: From extro- + -version. As a variant of extraversion, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's use of the (then nonstandard) spelling extrovert in her publication "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte" (1918).

s.d: (psychology) an extroverted disposition; concern with what is outside the self
(obsolete, uncountable) The state or quality of being extroverted or an extrovert: Consideration of the material world as an aid to spiritual insight.
x: in mystical Divinity... a scattering or distracting ones thoughts upon exterior objects.
The turning of the eye of the mind from [Christ] to outward things [mystics] call Extroversion.

s.d: (uncountable) The state or quality of being extroverted or an extrovert: The condition of being inside out, especially in relation to the bladder.
x: In extroversion of the bladder the anterior part of this organ is more or less completely wanting.

s.d: (informal, uncountable) The state or quality of being extroverted or an extrovert: A personality orientation towards others and things outside oneself; behavior expressing such orientation.
x: Extroversion is the thrusting out of the mind on to life, the use of the mind in practical affairs, the pouring out of the libido on external objects.
In a genre characterized by brassy extroversion, The Dead is a quiet revolutionary: a musical that dares to be diffident.

s.d: directed outward; marked by interest in others or concerned with external reality
Synonym of extroverted.

extrovert.e: Alteration of earlier extravert (by influence of introvert), from German Extravert, popularized in psychology by Phyllis Blanchard's 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte". By surface analysis, extro- + -vert.

s.d: (psychology) a person concerned more with practical realities than with inner thoughts and feelings
(informal) An extroverted person: one who is outgoing, sociable, and concerned with outer affairs.
x: To see your identity in any single trait – introvert, extrovert, or neurotic – is to limit your life.
Natural extroverts, they burst into a room with the barely contained energy of a pair of puppy dogs.

s.d: To turn or thrust outwards.
x: The external and combustible Sulphur... is... protruded and extroverted.

s.d: being concerned with the social and physical environment

extroverted.e: A variant spelling of extraverted. Popularized as a psychological term by Phyllis Blanchard's use of extrovert in her 1918 "Psycho-Analytic Study of August Comte", from extrovert + -ed.

s.d: not introspective; examining what is outside yourself
at ease in talking to others
being concerned with the social and physical environment
Turned or thrust outwards, especially
x: The external and combustible Sulphur... is... protruded and extroverted.

s.d: (informal) Turned or thrust outwards, especially:: Of or characteristic of the personality of an extrovert: outgoing, sociable.
x: She's very extroverted. She's always out meeting new people and looking for new experiences.
This subtle but important distinction means otroverts can blend into both introverted and extroverted environments without fully belonging to either.

s.d: being somewhat extroverted
being concerned with the social and physical environment

extrude.e:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰ
Proto-Indo-European *-s
Proto-Indo-European *h₁éǵʰs
Proto-Italic *eks
Latin ex
Latin ex-
Proto-Indo-European *trewd-der.
Proto-Italic *troudō
Latin trūdō
Latin extrūderebor.
English extrude
Borrowed from Latin extrūdere.

s.d: form or shape by forcing through an opening
x: extrude steel

s.d: To push or thrust out.
x: Fire salamanders, which are common on forested hillsides in southern and central Europe, extrude secretions onto their skin containing a neurotoxic alkaloid, Samandarin, when they think they are under attack.
When a printer is extruding and has open spaces in a layer, printers pull the filament back so that stringing does not occur.

s.d: To expel; to drive off.

extrusion.e: Mid-16th century from Latin extrūdere, from ex- (“out”) + trūdere (“to thrust”).

s.d: something that bulges out or is protuberant or projects from its surroundings
x: the gun in his pocket made an obvious bulge
the hump of a camel

s.d: squeezing out by applying pressure
x: an unexpected extrusion of toothpaste from the bottom of the tube
the expulsion of pus from the pimple

s.d: (uncountable) A manufacturing process where a billet of material is pushed and/or drawn through a die to create a shaped rod, rail or pipe.
(uncountable) An item formed by the process of extrusion.
(uncountable) A process through which a virus leaves its host cell by fusing with that cell's plasma membrane.
Rock which has been formed through volcanic extrusion.
of rock material; forced out while molten through cracks in the earth's surface
Jutting out; extruding.
Of rocks: forced, while in a plastic or molten state, on to the Earth's surface to lie atop existing rocks.

exuberance.e: From French exubérance, from Latin exuberantia (“superabundance”), from exuberare (“to grow thickly, to abound”); from ex- (“out”) + uber (“udder”), which would have originally referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

s.d: joyful enthusiasm
overflowing with eager enjoyment or approval
(uncountable) The quality of being exuberant; cheerful or vigorous enthusiasm; liveliness.
x: Tottenham's desire for a win against a Norwich side playing with energy and exuberance made for an enthralling, end-to-end game.

s.d: (uncountable) An instance of exuberant behaviour.
(uncountable) An overflowing quantity; superfluousness.
x: an exuberance of branches in a plant

s.d: (uncountable) An abundance of wealth.

exuberant.e: From Middle French exubérant, from Latin exūberāns, the present active participle of exūberō (“be abundant”). Put together from ex (“out”), and uber (“udder”), and originally would have referred to a cow or she-goat which was making so much milk that it naturally dripped or sprayed from the udder.

s.d: joyously unrestrained
unrestrained, especially with regard to feelings
x: extravagant praise
exuberant compliments

s.d: produced or growing in extreme abundance
x: their riotous blooming

s.d: Very cheery and peppy; extremely cheerful, energetic and enthusiastic.
x: exuberant feeling
He was a man of exuberant fancy, and, withal of an authority so irresistible that, at his will, he turned his varied fancies into facts.

s.d: (literary) Abundant, luxuriant.
x: exuberant foliage
It pencilled each flower with rich and variegated hues, and threw over its exuberant foliage a vesture of emerald green.

s.d: Unusually proliferative, widespread or extreme, particularly in relation to a disease, immune reaction, or tissue

exuberantly.e:
Etymology tree
English exuberant
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English exuberantly
From exuberant + -ly.

s.d: in an exuberant manner
x: the exuberantly baroque decoration of the church

s.d: in an ebullient manner
x: Khrushchev ebulliently promised to supply rockets for the protection of Cuba against American aggression

exuberate.e: From Latin exuberatus, past participle of exuberare. See exuberant (“adjective”).

s.d: to express great joy
x: Who cannot exult in Spring?

s.d: (obsolete) To abound; to be in great abundance.
x: that vast confluence and immensity, that exuberates in God

s.d: (archaic) To develop into (something), by an exuberance of growth.
x: ‘He might perhaps have become one, if he had had time to ripen, (smiling.) He might have exuberated into an Atheist.’

s.d: To delight, to make exuberant
x: It's fun, thrilling, and exuberating.

exudate.e:
Etymology tree
English exude
Proto-Indo-European *-h₂
Proto-Indo-European *-éh₂
Proto-Indo-European *-tós
Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂tos
Proto-Italic *-ātos
Latin -ātusder.
English -ate
English exudate
From exude + -ate (noun-forming suffix).

s.d: a substance that oozes out from plant pores
A fluid that has exuded from somewhere; especially one that has exuded from a pore of an animal or plant.
x: The whitish lines of exudate seem at times to penetrate even between the straight tubes . . .
When this is done, one should leave the poppy for some time, then return to it and gather any further exudate.

s.d: release (a liquid) in drops or small quantities
x: exude sweat through the pores

s.d: (obsolete) To exude.
x: There is, hereto, no derivation of the seminal parts, nor any passage from hence, unto the vessels of ejaculation: some perforations only in the part itself, through which the humour included doth exudate

exudation.e:
Etymology tree
English exude
Proto-Indo-European *-tis
Proto-Indo-European *-Hō
Proto-Indo-European *-tiHō
Proto-Italic *-tiō
Latin -tiō
Latin -ātiōlbor.

English -ation
English exudation
From exude + -ation.

s.d: a substance that oozes out from plant pores
the process of exuding; the slow escape of liquids from blood vessels through pores or breaks in the cell membranes
(uncountable) The act or process of exuding.
x: In severe burns, the body loses large amounts of nitrogen, in the urine and by exudation from the burned body surface.

s.d: (uncountable) Something that is exuded.
x: The skin must be frequently and thoroughly washed, occasionally with warm water and soap, to remove the oily exudations upon its surface.
The car was parked in close to the rustic fence, under the lime trees, and their sticky exudations had already stippled the windscreen.

exude.e: Latin exudāre, exsudāre (“to sweat out”), from ex- (“out, out of”) + sudāre (“to sweat”), from Proto-Indo-European *sweyd-.

s.d: release (a liquid) in drops or small quantities
x: exude sweat through the pores

s.d: make apparent by one's mood or behavior
x: She exudes great confidence

s.d: To discharge through pores or incisions, as moisture or other liquid matter; to give out.
x: There are five hundred and fifty-five trees, and they exude the sweetest odours

s.d: To flow out through the pores.
x: The molten glass exudes into the space outside the outer crucible, and a filament is pulled from the exudant to form a cored glass fiber.

s.d: To give off or radiate a certain quality or emotion, often strongly.
x: Wearing that suit, Jasper just exudes class.

exult.e: From Middle French exulter, from Latin exsultō, frequentative of exsiliō (“jump up”), from ex- + saliō (“jump, leap”).

s.d: feel extreme happiness or elation
to express great joy
x: Who cannot exult in Spring?

s.d: To rejoice; to be very happy, especially in triumph; to triumph (over).
x: I took a deep breath; a locomotive howled across-the darkness, Mobile-bound. So were we. I took off my shirt and exulted.

exultant.e: From Latin exsultāns, present participle of exsultō (“rejoice; boast”). See also exult.

s.d: joyful and proud especially because of triumph or success
x: rejoicing crowds filled the streets on VJ Day
a triumphal success

s.d: Very happy, especially at someone else's defeat or failure.

exultantly.e:
Etymology tree
English exultant
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English exultantly
From exultant + -ly.

s.d: in an exultant manner
x: it was exultingly easy

exultation.e: From Middle English exultacion, from Old French exultacion, from Latin exsultātiō, exsultātiōnem.

s.d: a feeling of extreme joy
the utterance of sounds expressing great joy
(uncountable) The act of exulting; great joy at success or victory, or at any advantage gained; rapturous delight
x: Strange that this idea carried with it something of exultation! so much does the pride of man rejoice in aught that marks him from his fellows, and little does it seem to matter whether that mark be for good or for evil.
You will experience the fun of life — the magic, the celebration, the exhilaration, and the exultation of your own spirit.

s.d: Synonym of exaltation (“A flock of doves, larks or skylarks”)
x: An exultation of larks rose from the fen itself.
Oh, look, our mam, there's a wisp of snipe and an exultation of skylarks flying over that clouder of cats!

s.d: exultation
x: Disappointments and sorrows have taught me the vanity of human expectations, quieted the exultings of youthful hope, and cooled the ardour of anxious desire.

s.d: joyful and proud especially because of triumph or success
x: rejoicing crowds filled the streets on VJ Day
a triumphal success

s.d: Showing exultation.

exultingly.e:
Etymology tree
English exulting
Middle English -ly
English -ly
English exultingly
From exulting + -ly.

s.d: in an exultant manner
x: it was exultingly easy

s.d: In an exulting manner; with joy at a success or triumph.
x:
Hark—even now she cries exultingly
The vengeful cry that tells of battle turned—
She laughed exultingly, and the boy felt cold and strangely troubled.

exurbia.e:
Etymology tree
English exurb
Latin -iader.
English -ia
English exurbia
From exurb + -ia.

s.d: a residential area outside of a city and beyond suburbia
(uncountable) A residential area beyond the suburbs.

exuviae.e: Learned borrowing from Latin exuviae, from exuō (“cast off, undress”).

s.d: cast-off skins or coverings of various organisms during ecdysis
(plural-only) The coverings of an animal that have been shed or cast off, particularly the molted exoskeletons of arthropods.
(historical, plural-only) Among the Ancient Romans, weaponry and equipment stripped from the person of a foe; booty.

exuvial.e: From Latin exuviae (“what is stripped”), from exuo (“shed, strip”).

s.d: of or relating to the cast-off skins or cuticles of various animals
Related to something sloughed off or stripped away.
x: The floor of the cave was covered with the exuvial remains of unknown creatures.

exuviate.e: From Latin exuviae (“what is shed”), from exuō (“cast off, strip”).

s.d: cast off hair, skin, horn, or feathers
x: our dog sheds every Spring

s.d: (rare) To shed or cast off a covering, especially a skin; to slough; to molt (moult).
x: Like any arthropod encased in a rigid exoskeleton, a trilobite must periodically moult, or exuviate, in order to grow.
